CausalChain: Downregulation of CPT2 in HCC -> Accumulation of acylcarnitines -> Disruption of mitochondrial fatty acid oxidation -> Altered energy metabolism in tumor cells -> Modulation of surrounding immune cell functions (e.g., reduced NK cell and CD4+ T cell effectiveness) -> Creation of an immune suppressive microenvironment -> Enhanced tumor progression
Hypothesis: In hepatocellular carcinoma, CPT2 deficiency‐induced accumulation of acylcarnitines contributes to the suppression of anti-tumor immune surveillance by impairing natural killer and CD4+ T cell functions; thus, targeting CPT2 activity or acylcarnitine levels may restore immune function and sensitize tumors to immunotherapy.
Abstract: Recent evidence suggests that the dysregulation of lipid metabolism in chronic liver diseases not only fuels tumor growth but also may impair anti‐tumor immunity. In hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), reduced fatty acid oxidation and downregulation of key enzymes such as carnitine palmitoyltransferase 2 (CPT2) lead to an accumulation of lipid intermediates like acylcarnitines. These metabolites may disrupt not just metabolic homeostasis in hepatocytes but also modulate the function of immune cells, potentially impairing natural killer (NK) cell and CD4+ T cell surveillance. Here, we propose a novel hypothesis that mitochondrial dysregulation of lipid oxidation, mediated by CPT2 downregulation and subsequent acylcarnitine accumulation in HCC, contributes to an immune‐suppressive tumor microenvironment. Interventions that restore CPT2 activity or target acylcarnitine accumulation may reverse immune dysfunction and enhance the efficacy of immunotherapies in liver cancer.
